You answer a question about the Human Protein Atlas by reading the atlas's own web pages, as a careful librarian would. You see each page you have opened as its sections (heading, size) and its links; you open sections to read them and follow links by their number to reach other pages.
Reply with JSON, one of:
{"open": [{"page": <page number>, "sections": [<section numbers>]}]} to read sections you have not read;
{"follow": [{"page": <page number>, "link": <link number>}]} to fetch pages (at most 3);
{"answer": {"text": "<your answer in plain prose>", "citations": [{"n": 1, "page": <page number>, "quote": "<exact text>"}], "not_found": "<the part of the question the pages did not answer, in a few words, or empty>"}}.
Answer only when every part of the question is covered by sections you have read. If a link plainly leads to a part you still lack (a milestone page, a release note, a news post, a methods page), follow it first, within the budget; a page's own subpages usually hold the detail its overview only names.
Write the answer as you would to a colleague: direct, in full sentences, with the numbers, names, dates and thresholds as the pages give them. Every sentence ends with the citation it rests on, written as [n]; a sentence may cite several, [1][2]. A sentence says no more than its citations say.
A citation is an exact span of page text: pick a start word and an end word on the page and copy everything between them character for character, the page's own spelling, capitalization, punctuation and mistakes included. Do not fix, shorten, join, reorder or translate anything; no ellipsis; one continuous passage of 15 to 600 characters. Shorter is safer: the one sentence or clause that carries the fact. A sentence that sums up a list or a table cites several short spans, given as a list: "quote": ["<span>", "<span>"], each one exact. Quote from section text you opened, never from link labels or from memory. Every citation is checked against the page; one that is not on the page exactly as written, or longer than 600 characters, is sent back to you with the page's text around it, and a sentence without a verified citation is not shown. not_found names only what the pages did not answer; it states no facts.

What you have read:
--- Page 1, section 0: Protein Atlas version 25.1
Single Cell The latest addition to the Single Cell resource is Deep Visual Proteomics (DVP) data. Cell-type resolved MS-based protein profiles across 27 different cell types, representing 14 different tissues, are integrated into the Single Cell resource. Selected Single Cell Type data are matched to the DVP samples to facilitate a side-by-side comparison of RNA and protein data, accompanied by specificity overlap and agreement scores for systematic RNA-to-protein comparisons. A total of 27 cell type shapes (with 3-5 replicates each), grouped into 24 cell types used for classifications, are included in this release. Tissue Quantitative proteomics profiles (MS-based) for bulk tissue samples are integrated to the Tissue resource. 20 different tissue types, overlapping with the DVP samples are integrated to the gene-summary pages, providing protein profiles for over 12,700 genes.

--- Page 1, section 1: Protein Atlas version 25.0
Twenty-fifth major release of the Human Protein Atlas with over 27,800 antibodies, targeting proteins from over 17,400 human genes (~88% of the human protein-coding genes). 9 separate resources with data covering various aspects of human protein-coding genes. Tissue & Cancer In total 3,937 proteins are validated with Enhanced validation strategies. 14 new antibodies were added. The standard IHC profiling of one antibody was updated and all tissue & cancer images were replaced with new data resulting from restaining of the antibody. Tissue The Tissue resource has expanded the extended protein profiling with eight new tissue samples, including e.g. choroid plexus, efferent ducts, ovary and different phases of placental development. Additional 277 proteins were validated with IHC on extended tissue samples. In total, 873 proteins have been validated on 29 different extended tissue samples. Multiplex tissue profiling has been updated with a new pancreas antibody panel used to study 77 proteins. Additional 22 proteins were studied in ciliated cells. In total, 1106 proteins have been analyzed using 8 antibody panels. New GTEx RNA-seq samples from blood vessels have been added to the consensus bulk RNA data. Brain Spatial transcriptomics data is now updated. Now 3 cerebellum section and 3 cerebral cortex samples (stereo-seq platform) are added. For each sample a crop including all tissue layers is included and the transcript counts for the main cell types (neurons/Purkinje cells, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia and vascular cells) are calculated for each layer for each sample. Single Cell The updated single cell type data represents 34 different tissue types, from 35 separate data sources. Brain cells are now represented by a subsampling of the brain single nuclei data (Siletti. K, et al.), separated into neuronal and non-neuronal (two cell UMAPs from the same data source). Eye is represented by a dataset of general eye-related cells, as well as a retina sample with only retinal cells (one tissue type but two separate sources and UMAPs). Other changes include: Adrenal gland, pituitary gland (single nuclei), epididymis and urinary bladder are newly added tissues, bronchus is removed, the data source is changed for PMBC/blood, bone marrow, esophagus, lymph node, pancreas, spleen, stomach. Single nuclei data is added to replace previous single cell data for adipose tissue, heart muscle, skeletal muscle and kidney. The updated data includes 154 different cell types representing the whole body, these are grouped into 53 main cell type groups for a better overview and categorization. Cell type specificity is calculated for both 154 cell types and the 53 cell type groups. The 15 color-coded cell icons, previously referred to as cell groups, are now called cell class. Tissue and cell types are now sorted based on the organ system on the tissue resource. Color codes are updated for cell types. Twenty-third major release of the Human Protein Atlas with over 27,500 antibodies, targeting proteins from over 17,200 human genes (~87% of the human protein-coding genes). 12 separate sections with data covering various aspect of human protein-coding genes. Interaction A new section containing protein-protein and metabolic interaction networks has been added. The Interaction section builds on the former Metabolic section with the addition of selected protein-protein interaction data from the EMBL-EBI IntAct database, and presents protein-protein interaction networks for 11351 genes together with metabolic maps for 2912 genes. The interaction networks are extendable and interactive and can be integrated with other data in the Atlas to highlight proteins according to custom made filters or pre-selected features such as subcellular location or tissue specificity. Protein 3D structures The structure section has been revised to allow for closer integration with relevant data in the Atlas. The experimentally determined structures from PDB have been temporarily removed and only predicted 3D structures from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database project are shown. A Protein Browser has been added that can be used to select individual splice variants and display protein related features such as known antigen sequences, transmembrane regions and InterPro domains on the structures. The possibility to highlight amino acid positions of population variants and variants with known clinical relevance as well as other features remains. Expression clustering A new clustering of genes was performed for the updated transcript data in the Tissue, Single Cell Type, Brain, Immune Cell and Cell Line sections, resulting in 83, 80, 56, 46 and 72 clusters, respectively, each classified according to common features in terms of main function, location and specificity. Tissue & Pathology In total 3942 proteins are validated with Enhanced validation strategies. 5 antibodies were omitted, 69 new antibodies were added. Tissue 351 proteins underwent multiplex protein profiling, where 192 were analyzed in 6 new cell types/cell states in testis. In total, 742 proteins have been analyzed in 16 cell types in testis and 5 cell types in kidney using multiplex protein profiling, based on overlap of antibody staining with cell/state specific markers. Brain For this version of the brain section we performed a detailed analysis and comparison of samples. Based clustering analysis we further improved the grouping of samples. We found that the ventromedial nucleus sample, previous group in thalamus, is the ventromedial nucleus of the hypothalamus and is now added to that region. The claustrum which is located between the cortex and basal ganglia was grouped in the basal ganglia, but based on similarities in gene expression is now moved the cerebral cortex group. We also identified that for Nucleus cuneatus some samples were named cuneate nucleus. This has now been corrected and samples are grouped as nucleus cuneatus. When performing our clustering analysis, we found a technical batch effect between RNAseq data based on Illumina and MGI platforms. Correcting for this technical bias affected many of the biological differences between regions of the brain. We therefore decided to separate samples generated on these two sequencing platforms and only normalize samples that have been sequenced using the same method. The consequence of this is that the prefrontal cortex dataset is separated from the rest of the brain samples and expression values of prefrontal cortex areas cannot directly be compared to other regions of the brain. Based on anatomy, function, and protein expression profiles we now organized individual subregions within the regions. For example, subregions in the basal ganglia are now organized as striatum, basal forebrain or globus pallidus. A new feature in the brain section is the UMAP based on distribution of protein coding transcripts in the human brain. This cluster data provides an overview of genes with similar distribution profile that often share functions (e.g. synaptic functions) or are expressed by specific cell types (e.g. oligodendrocytes or immune-cells). Single Cell Type Single cell RNA data from 1 new tissue (Fallopian tube) was added, all previously published data was revised, and Ovary was replaced by a new dataset. All genes were mapped from Ensembl 103 to Ensembl 109. This resulted in a total of 81 cell types from 31 different human tissues including peripheral mononuclear cells (PBMCs).
